title: Cigar Party
concept: Combining a range check with a special-case flag
brief: Decides if a cigar count is good for a party, with looser rules on weekends.
description: Write a function that says whether a party has a good number of cigars. Normally that means somewhere between 40 and 60, inclusive. On weekends there's no upper limit at all, so as long as there are at least 40, it's fine.
hints: Handle the weekend case and the regular case as two separate branches.
On a weekend only the lower bound of 40 matters; on a normal day both 40 and 60 matter.
explainer: When it's a weekend the function only checks the lower bound, and otherwise it checks the full 40-to-60 range, which matches how the party rules loosen up on weekends.

title: Date Fashion
brief: Rates a date's chances from two fashion scores, letting a low score veto everything.
description: Write a function that takes two fashion scores from 0 to 10, one for you and one for your date, and returns how promising the date looks. If either score is 2 or lower, the date is doomed no matter what. Otherwise, if either score is 8 or higher, things look great. If neither of those applies, it's just an average date.
hints: Check the 'doomed' condition (a score of 2 or less) before you check the 'great' condition.
Once you've ruled out the doomed case, checking for a score of 8 or more is straightforward.
explainer: Testing the low-score veto first means a great score can never rescue a date where someone scored 2 or below, and only after clearing that check does a high score bump the result up to 8.

title: Squirrel Play
concept: Range checks that shift with a flag
brief: Decides if it's warm enough for squirrels to play, with a higher heat tolerance in summer.
description: Write a function that decides if the temperature is comfortable enough for squirrels to be out playing. Normally that's anywhere from 60 to 90 degrees, inclusive. But in the summer, squirrels are used to the heat, so the top of that range stretches all the way up to 100.
hints: The lower bound of 60 never changes; only the upper bound depends on the season.
Write one range check for summer and a different one for the rest of the year.
explainer: Both branches share the same 60-degree floor, but the summer branch raises the ceiling to 100 instead of 90, matching the wider comfortable range in hot months.

title: Caught Speeding
concept: Layered range checks with a shifting threshold
brief: Turns a driving speed into a ticket severity, giving a 5 mph birthday cushion.
description: Write a function that scores how serious a speeding ticket would be. The normal speed limit is 60. Going up to 20 over that limit earns a small ticket, and anything beyond that earns a big one; staying at or under the limit means no ticket at all. On the driver's birthday, every one of those thresholds gets 5 mph more forgiving.
hints: Compute one 'birthday bonus' number (0 or 5) first, then reuse it in both threshold checks.
Compare against 60 plus the bonus for the first threshold, and 80 plus the bonus for the second.
explainer: Adding the same birthday bonus to both the 60 and 80 thresholds shifts the whole scale by 5 mph at once, so every ticket level becomes 5 mph more forgiving on a birthday.

title: Sorta Sum
concept: Overriding a computed value inside a range
brief: Adds two numbers, but rounds any teen-sized total up to 20.
description: Write a function that adds two numbers together, but if that total lands anywhere from 10 through 19, it gets bumped up to exactly 20 instead. Any other total is returned exactly as computed.
hints: Add the two numbers first and store the result before deciding what to return.
Use a single range check, 10 <= total <= 19, to catch every 'teen' total.
explainer: The sum is computed once and then checked against the 10-to-19 window; any total that falls inside gets swapped for 20, and everything else passes through unchanged.

title: Alarm Clock
concept: Nested conditions over a day-of-week code
brief: Picks a wake-up time based on the day of the week and whether it's vacation.
description: Write a function that returns a wake-up time as text. The day is given as a number where 0 means Sunday and 6 means Saturday, with 1 through 5 being the weekdays. Normally weekdays wake up at '7:00' and weekends sleep in until '10:00'. On vacation, weekends stay the same but weekdays get to sleep in a bit later, until '9:00'.
hints: First figure out whether the day number falls in the weekday range 1 through 5.
Vacation only changes the weekday wake-up time; the weekend time is always '10:00'.
explainer: The weekday check is computed once and reused, and only the weekday branch changes between vacation and non-vacation, since weekends always sleep in until '10:00' either way.

title: Love 6
brief: Checks if the number 6 shows up as either value, their sum, or their difference.
description: Write a function that returns True if the number 6 is somehow connected to two given numbers: either one of them is 6, or adding them gives 6, or the distance between them (ignoring which is bigger) is 6.
solution:
def love6(a, b):
    return a == 6 or b == 6 or a + b == 6 or abs(a - b) == 6
hints: You can chain several conditions together with 'or' in one return statement.
abs(a - b) gives you the distance between the two numbers no matter which one is larger.
explainer: Chaining the four checks with 'or' means the function returns True as soon as any single one of them is satisfied, which covers every way the number 6 could be connected to a and b.

title: In 1 To 10
concept: A flag that flips a range check inside-out
brief: Checks if a number is in 1-10, or flips to checking the outside of that range.
description: Write a function that normally checks whether a number is somewhere from 1 to 10, inclusive. When a special flag is turned on, it instead checks the opposite: whether the number sits at or beyond one of those two edges, 1 or 10.
hints: Write the normal 1-to-10 range check first, then think about what its 'opposite' looks like.
The opposite of being strictly inside the range is touching or passing one of its two edges.
explainer: When outside_mode is off, the function uses a plain 1-to-10 range check; when it's on, it instead checks whether n has reached or gone past either edge of that range, which covers everything the plain check would call False plus the edges themselves.

title: Near Ten
concept: Using remainder to measure distance from round numbers
brief: Checks if a number is within 2 of a multiple of ten.
description: Write a function that returns True if a number is close to a round multiple of ten, meaning it's no more than 2 away from one, either just before it or just after it.
solution:
def near_ten(num):
    return num % 10 <= 2 or num % 10 >= 8
hints: num % 10 tells you how far num is past the most recent multiple of ten.
A remainder of 0, 1, or 2 means it's just after a multiple of ten; a remainder of 8 or 9 means it's just before the next one.
explainer: The remainder after dividing by 10 shows how far a number sits past the last multiple of ten, so a small remainder or one close to 10 both mean the number is within 2 of some multiple of ten.
